results.notes: Full title is 'The Measure of Man: Human Factors in Design', published by Whitney Library of Design (New York). Most authoritative sources (Britannica, library catalogs, IDSA) give 1960; a Cooper Hewitt object record and a few secondary sources say 1959, so narration should say 'around 1960' or simply '1960' and avoid asserting a month. It was issued as a portfolio of anthropometric charts (including two life-size Joe/Josephine figure charts), not a conventional prose book. Revised 1967; later expanded by Dreyfuss Associates into the Humanscale portfolios (MIT Press) and 'The Measure of Man and Woman' (1990s). Dreyfuss himself used the period term 'human engineering'; 'ergonomics'/'human factors' are the modern labels.

results.claim: Dreyfuss designed telephones for Bell/Western Electric (e.g. the model 302 in 1937 and the model 500 in 1949).

sources.title: The 302 (Object of the Day)
sources.supports: States Dreyfuss began consulting for Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1930, that his work with Bell engineers produced the 302 in 1937, and that the 500 debuted in 1949 as a lighter plastic redesign.

sources.title: Model 302 / 500 telephone collection record
sources.supports: Museum object record attributing the Bell System telephone design to Dreyfuss, manufactured by Western Electric.

sources.title: Model 500 telephone
sources.supports: Development began 1946 by the Dreyfuss firm with Bell Labs and Western Electric; AT&T announced it in 1949 with ~4,000 field-trial sets; first ~23,000 production sets released to Bell operating companies in 1950; standard US desk phone until the 1984 divestiture.

results.notes: Precise framing: the client was Bell Telephone Laboratories (AT&T's research arm) and the manufacturer was Western Electric, so say 'designed for Bell Labs, built by Western Electric' rather than 'for Western Electric'. The 302 went into production in 1937 (cast-metal housing, switched to thermoplastic around 1941); some sources credit Bell Labs engineer George Lum for its engineering, with Dreyfuss shaping the form in collaboration with Bell's engineers. The 500 was publicly announced/field-trialed in 1949 but reached production and customers in 1950, so 'introduced in 1949' is correct for the debut, while 'in homes from 1950' is the safer phrasing for availability. Roughly 93 million 500-series sets were made through 1984 (secondary-source figure).

results.claim: Human factors / ergonomics research grew substantially in the WWII era, including studies of aircraft cockpit controls (e.g. Alphonse Chapanis and Paul Fitts).

sources.title: Alphonse Chapanis
sources.supports: Chapanis (Yale PhD 1943) was the first psychologist at the Army Air Forces Aero Medical Laboratory at Wright Field; traced gear-up landing accidents in B-17s, B-25s and P-47s to confusable side-by-side gear and flap controls and introduced shape coding; co-authored the first human factors textbook in 1949.

sources.title: Fitts and Jones' Analysis of Pilot Error: 40 Years Later
sources.supports: Academic paper on the 1947 Fitts & Jones Aero Medical Laboratory study of 460 'pilot-error' experiences, which reframed cockpit control errors as design problems.

sources.title: Pilot Error? Chapanis and the Shape of Things to Come
sources.supports: Narrative account of the wartime B-17 flap/landing-gear confusion and Chapanis's shape-coding fix (wheel-shaped gear knob, wedge-shaped flap knob).

results.notes: Timeline nuance: Chapanis's cockpit-control work at Wright Field was during the war (from 1943). Paul Fitts arrived at Wright Field in July 1945 (with Walter Grether) to form the lab's psychology branch, and the famous Fitts & Jones 460-error 'pilot error' study is a 1947 postwar memorandum report (TSEAA-694-12), so narration should say 'WWII and its immediate aftermath' rather than dating Fitts's study to the war itself. Chapanis's formulation was 'designer error', not 'pilot error'. The first human factors textbook, Applied Experimental Psychology: Human Factors in Engineering Design (Chapanis, Garner & Morgan), appeared in 1949; the UK Ergonomics Research Society also formed in 1949 (Waterson 2011). Avoid the popular claims that 'accidents dropped to zero overnight' and that shape coding is 'still legally required' - neither is supported by a primary source in the results. Exact hardware details (wedge vs. triangle, rubber strips) vary across sources, so keep descriptions general.

challenges.claim: Dreyfuss was an American industrial designer associated with human factors/ergonomics and anthropometric data (later "The Measure of Man", 1960).
challenges.reason: Holds. Dreyfuss (born New York, 1904; died Pasadena area, 1972) was American; 'The Measure of Man: Human Factors in Design' was published by the Whitney Library of Design, New York, in 1960, as a folio with the life-size 'Joe' and 'Josephine' charts. Two nuances worth carrying into the wording to avoid over-attribution: (a) the 'Joe and Josephine' figures were first introduced in 'Designing for People' (1955), and (b) the anthropometric drawings were drafted by Dreyfuss's long-time associate Alvin R. Tilley (per Cooper Hewitt), drawing on US military and fashion-industry data. Also note that Flinchum & Meyer (Winterthur Portfolio, 2017) argue Dreyfuss did not actually rely on anthropometric measurements in his telephone work, so the ergonomics association belongs to the firm's published charts rather than to every product. 'Associated with' is accurate as stated.
challenges.better_wording: Dreyfuss (1904–1972) was an American industrial designer whose office, Henry Dreyfuss Associates, popularized anthropometric data for designers: the 'Joe and Josephine' figures appeared in Designing for People (1955) and became the life-size charts of The Measure of Man (Whitney Library of Design, 1960), drafted largely by associate Alvin R. Tilley.

challenges.claim: Dreyfuss designed telephones for Bell/Western Electric (e.g. the model 302 in 1937 and the model 500 in 1949).
challenges.reason: The model 500 part holds: Dreyfuss's firm designed the Western Electric 500, which debuted in 1949 (field trials of 4,000 sets in 1949; production units dated Q1 1949) and became the Bell System's standard desk set from 1950. The model 302 attribution is the problem. The Smithsonian's object record for the Model 302 lists Bell Telephone Laboratories engineer George R. Lum (1889–1989) as designer, with Dreyfuss only as a contributor; Lum held the 1935 design patent 'Desk Stand for a Hand Telephone'. Russell Flinchum and Ralph Meyer's peer-reviewed article 'Henry Dreyfuss and Bell Telephones' (Winterthur Portfolio 51:4, 2017, pp. 173–200) explicitly sets out to dispel the myth that Dreyfuss designed the 302, using Dreyfuss-firm insider sources, and credits Lum; Wikipedia's Model 302 article now follows this. Some older Cooper Hewitt pages still say 'designed by Henry Dreyfuss', so the attribution is contested, but current scholarship and the Smithsonian record favor Lum. Presenting the 302 as a Dreyfuss design is over-attribution. (Also, Dreyfuss had consulted for Bell Labs since 1930, so the 302 was not the start of the relationship.)
challenges.better_wording: Dreyfuss consulted for Bell Telephone Laboratories from 1930, and his firm's landmark telephone was the Western Electric model 500 (introduced 1949; the Bell System's standard desk set from 1950). The earlier model 302 (1937), long credited to Dreyfuss, is now attributed by the Smithsonian and by Flinchum & Meyer (Winterthur Portfolio, 2017) to Bell Labs engineer George R. Lum, with Dreyfuss's office contributing at most.

challenges.claim: Human factors / ergonomics research grew substantially in the WWII era, including studies of aircraft cockpit controls (e.g. Alphonse Chapanis and Paul Fitts).
challenges.reason: Holds. Chapanis (Yale PhD 1943) served as the first psychologist at the Army Air Forces Aero Medical Laboratory, Wright Field, where he diagnosed B-17 gear/flap control confusions and introduced shape-coded knobs; in Britain the MRC Applied Psychology Unit (est. 1944) ran the 'Cambridge Cockpit' studies, and Waterson (Ergonomics, 2011) traces UK ergonomics directly to WWII research. One dating nuance: Fitts and Jones's landmark 'Analysis of factors contributing to 460 "pilot-error" experiences in operating aircraft controls' is Aero Medical Laboratory Memorandum Report TSEAA-694-12, dated 1947, i.e. immediately post-war (analyzing wartime incidents), and the word 'ergonomics' itself was coined only in 1949. Secondary sources also disagree on whether Chapanis's B-17 fix was 1942 or 1943, so avoid giving a precise year for it. 'WWII era' as a loose phrase covers this; a tighter wording should say 'during and immediately after WWII'.
challenges.better_wording: Human factors research expanded sharply during and immediately after World War II: Alphonse Chapanis, at the Army Air Forces' Aero Medical Laboratory, showed that B-17 'pilot error' gear-up landings stemmed from identical, adjacent gear and flap controls, and Paul Fitts and Richard Jones's 1947 analysis of 460 control-operation errors generalized the finding that many 'pilot errors' were cockpit design errors.

results.claim: Ivan Sutherland created Sketchpad in 1963 (as his MIT PhD thesis) on the TX-2 computer at MIT Lincoln Laboratory.

sources.title: The Remarkable Ivan Sutherland
sources.supports: States that in January 1963 Sutherland completed his PhD on the system he created on the TX-2, Sketchpad; notes he met TX-2 designer Wesley Clark at Lincoln Laboratory and proposed using the machine for engineering-drawing software.

sources.title: The TX-2 Computer and Sketchpad
sources.supports: Lincoln Laboratory's own retrospective: the TX-2 was an experimental digital computer created at MIT in 1958, Sketchpad ran on it, and much of computer graphics began on the TX-2.

sources.title: Sketchpad, a man-machine graphical communication system (PhD thesis record)
sources.supports: Catalog record of the 1963 MIT Department of Electrical Engineering PhD thesis, submitted January 7, 1963, with Claude E. Shannon as thesis supervisor.

results.notes: Dating nuance: 1963 is the thesis year, not the start of the work. The Sketchpad program itself was built on the TX-2 during roughly 1961-1962 (CHM holds Sketchpad footage catalogued circa 1961); the thesis was submitted January 7, 1963 (CHM marks Jan 7 as the day Sutherland 'introduced' Sketchpad) and a companion paper appeared at the Spring Joint Computer Conference in 1963. Safe phrasing: 'completed in 1963' or 'presented in his 1963 MIT PhD thesis' rather than 'invented in 1963.' Thesis supervisor was Claude Shannon (committee included Marvin Minsky and Steven Coons) - a nice detail if wanted. The TX-2 was built at Lincoln Laboratory under Wesley Clark and became operational in 1958; Lincoln Laboratory is an MIT lab but is located off the main Cambridge campus (in Lexington, MA - this location was not confirmed by the search results, only by general knowledge, so avoid stating it unless independently checked). The thesis was republished in 2003 by the University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory as Technical Report UCAM-CL-TR-574, which is the freely available edition most people read today. Sutherland received the 1988 ACM Turing Award citing Sketchpad.

results.claim: Sketchpad used a light pen to draw and manipulate geometric shapes directly on a CRT display.

sources.title: Sketchpad
sources.supports: Describes Sketchpad as the first interactive computer-graphics program, running on the TX-2 at MIT's Lincoln Laboratory; it displayed graphics on the CRT display and a light pen was used to manipulate the line objects, much like a modern mouse.

sources.title: 1963 (Computer History Museum Timeline)
sources.supports: Describes Sketchpad as an interactive, real-time computer drawing system in which a user could create and manipulate graphical figures with a light pen; calls the thesis a seminal basis for later graphical user interfaces.

sources.title: Light pen and interface box (prototype) - CHM Revolution
sources.supports: Establishes that light pens were developed about 1952 to select points on the display of MIT's Whirlwind computer - i.e., the device predates Sketchpad.

results.notes: Core claim is solid: drawing and editing of lines, circles/arcs and composite figures with a light pen on the TX-2's CRT, including geometric constraints (parallel, perpendicular, equal length) applied to the drawing. Nuances: (1) Sutherland did not invent the light pen - it dates to MIT's Whirlwind (~1952) and was used on the SAGE air-defense system; Sketchpad popularized it as a drawing/pointing device. Avoid narration implying the pen was his invention. (2) The light pen was not the only input: Sketchpad also relied on push-buttons and knobs on the TX-2 console (e.g., to start a line, apply constraints, zoom/rotate), so 'directly' should mean on-screen pointing, not pen-only control. (3) The light pen worked by sensing when the CRT's beam lit the spot under it, which is why the system had to track the pen's position relative to its prior position (the 'INK'/tracking cross described in the thesis). (4) If the film uses the familiar black-and-white demonstration footage, that is mostly from the 1964 MIT 'Science Reporter' episode 42 'Computer Sketchpad', in which Timothy Johnson (MIT Mechanical Engineering) operates the system at Lincoln Laboratory, not Sutherland himself - credits for that episode vary across sources, so attribute carefully.

results.claim: Early computer interaction commonly used punched cards and later typed commands at terminals; typical users had to learn specialized command languages.

sources.title: Punched Cards - CHM Revolution
sources.supports: States that until the 1970s punched cards remained the primary computer input and storage medium for data and, later, software programs.

sources.title: Human-machine interface
sources.supports: Describes the batch (punch-card) interface as tedious and error-prone, followed by command-line interfaces that let users interactively issue commands, which were an improvement but did not take full advantage of human perceptual and learning abilities.

sources.title: Direct Manipulation: Definition
sources.supports: Explains that command-line interfaces require users to recall both command names (e.g., 'mv') and the names of the objects involved - recall rather than recognition - which is the usability basis for saying users had to learn command languages.

results.notes: Broadly accurate as a sweep of interface eras, but the narration should respect three nuances. (1) In the batch/punched-card era (1950s-1960s) 'typical users' generally did not interact with the computer at all: they handed card decks to operators and waited an hour or more for printed output (Britannica, batch processing); the specialized knowledge was of coding sheets, job-control cards and programming languages, not 'commands' in the interactive sense. (2) Typed commands at terminals arrived with time-sharing - first described in 1959 by Strachey and McCarthy, with MIT's CTSS as an early system (1961) - initially on teletypes and only widely on video terminals (VDTs) from the mid-1970s. (3) The eras overlapped heavily rather than succeeding one another cleanly: punched cards stayed in use into the 1970s, and interactive graphics like Sketchpad (1963) and Whirlwind/SAGE displays predate most people's exposure to command-line terminals. So 'and later typed commands' is fine as a general arc, but avoid implying Sketchpad came after the command-line era or that card-era users typed anything. Don Norman's jnd.org piece ('UI Breakthrough - Command Line Interfaces', https://jnd.org/ui-breakthrough-command-line-interfaces/) also supports the framing that GUIs replaced arbitrary memorized commands with direct manipulation.

challenges.claim: Ivan Sutherland created Sketchpad in 1963 (as his MIT PhD thesis) on the TX-2 computer at MIT Lincoln Laboratory.
challenges.reason: The core facts hold: Sutherland was an MIT EE doctoral student (advisor Claude Shannon), Sketchpad ran on Wes Clark's TX-2 at Lincoln Laboratory, the thesis 'Sketchpad: A Man-Machine Graphical Communication System' is dated January 1963 (issued as Lincoln Laboratory Technical Report 296, 30 Jan 1963), and the PhD was awarded in 1963. The only nuance is dating: the program itself was built during 1961-62 (Britannica dates the first version to 1961; Wikipedia says 'invented Sketchpad in 1962'; Sutherland was at Lincoln Lab 1960-63). '1963' is the thesis/publication and public-demo date (AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference, spring 1963), not the year the software was written. Also, Sketchpad was the subject of the thesis rather than literally 'the thesis'. Not a concrete error, but worth tightening.
challenges.better_wording: Ivan Sutherland built Sketchpad in 1961-62 on the TX-2 computer at MIT Lincoln Laboratory and described it in his January 1963 MIT PhD thesis, demonstrating it publicly at the Spring Joint Computer Conference that year.

challenges.claim: Sketchpad used a light pen to draw and manipulate geometric shapes directly on a CRT display.
challenges.reason: Accurate. Sutherland's thesis describes using the light pen to indicate positions and point at existing drawing parts on the TX-2's 9-inch CRT, drawing points, line segments and circular arcs and applying geometric constraints. Two nuances: (1) the pen was not the sole input - commands were issued with a box of pushbuttons ('draw', 'move', etc.), a bank of toggle switches, and four knobs that panned and zoomed the picture, so the pen selected and positioned while buttons chose the operation; (2) the light pen was not new - MIT's Whirlwind used a 'light gun' around 1952 and SAGE operators used one in the mid-1950s, so Sketchpad's novelty was the software, not the device. The claim does not assert otherwise, so it stands.
challenges.better_wording: Sketchpad let the user draw and manipulate geometric shapes directly on a CRT with a light pen (a device inherited from Whirlwind and SAGE), used together with pushbuttons and knobs to choose operations and pan or zoom the drawing.

challenges.claim: Early computer interaction commonly used punched cards and later typed commands at terminals; typical users had to learn specialized command languages.
challenges.reason: Holds as a general characterization. Batch processing with punched-card decks dominated mainframe computing from the 1950s, with programmers handing decks to operators and waiting for output; time-sharing systems then let users type commands at teletype-style terminals; and command-line interfaces are described in HCI histories as designed for trained experts who had to recall commands. One sequencing nuance: 'later' overstates the separation. Typed-command interaction via time-sharing began at MIT with CTSS (prototype demonstrated November 1961, so before Sketchpad's 1963 thesis), while punched-card batch work persisted well into the 1970s; the two modes overlapped for roughly two decades. Also 'typical users' in the batch era were mostly programmers and operators rather than end users.
challenges.better_wording: Early computer interaction commonly meant submitting punched-card decks for batch processing; from the early 1960s time-sharing let people type commands at terminals instead, though both modes coexisted for years, and either way users had to learn specialized command languages.

results.claim: Douglas Engelbart and his SRI team gave the demonstration later called "The Mother of All Demos" on December 9, 1968, in San Francisco (Fall Joint Computer Conference).

sources.title: Firsts: The Demo - Doug Engelbart Institute
sources.supports: 90-minute live public demonstration on December 9, 1968 by Engelbart and his SRI Augmentation Research Center group at a session of the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco.

sources.title: 1968 "Mother of All Demos" Forecasted Much of the Technology We Use Every Day
sources.supports: On December 9, 1968 Engelbart and team presented live to a packed house at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco; the 'mother of all demos' label was applied later ('as it has since been dubbed').

sources.title: Net@50: Did Engelbart's "Mother of All Demos" Launch the Connected World?
sources.supports: Engelbart's team presented at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco on December 9, 1968 to an audience of roughly 1,000.

results.notes: Date, city and conference are solid. Nuances: (1) The nickname was applied retroactively; Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mother_of_All_Demos) credits Andy van Dam repeating the phrase in 1995 when introducing Engelbart at the Vannevar Bush Symposium at MIT, so narration should say 'later called' or 'since dubbed', never that it was called that in 1968. (2) Venue naming is inconsistent across sources: 'Civic Auditorium' (now Bill Graham Civic Auditorium; used by the Engelbart Institute and SRI alumni newsletter), 'Brooks Hall' (CHM blog, 1968 IEEE GRID listing), and 'Convention Center' (Engelbart MouseSite). Both halls are in the San Francisco Civic Center complex, and the IEEE Milestone page (https://ethw.org/Milestones:Public_Demonstration_of_Online_Systems_and_Personal_Computing,_1968) notes its own 'Brooks Hall' wording should read 'San Francisco Civic Auditorium'. Safest narration: 'at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco's Civic Center' or simply 'in San Francisco'. (3) The official session title was 'A research center for augmenting human intellect'; the system was NLS (oN-Line System). (4) Length is usually given as ~90 minutes (some say 100). (5) One on-screen outline on dougengelbart.org is dated December 8, but the Institute's main pages, SRI and CHM all use December 9; keep December 9.

results.claim: The 1968 demo showed a mouse, hypertext links, on-screen text editing, windows, and real-time collaboration/video conferencing with remote colleagues.

sources.title: 1968 "Mother of All Demos" Forecasted Much of the Technology We Use Every Day
sources.supports: The demo debuted the mouse controlling a networked system to demonstrate hypertext linking, real-time text editing, multiple windows with flexible view control, and shared-screen teleconferencing; SRI also says Engelbart hosted the first videoconferencing session during the demo.

sources.title: Douglas C. Engelbart - CHM Profile
sources.supports: NLS showed 'actual instances of, or precursors to' hypertext, shared-screen collaboration, multiple windows, on-screen video teleconferencing, and the mouse as an input device.

sources.title: The Mother of All Demos
sources.supports: Two microwave links provided live two-way video between the SRI lab in Menlo Park and the conference hall; the workstation in San Francisco was connected to the SDS 940 computer in Menlo Park via homemade modems; collaborative real-time editing and video conferencing were demonstrated.

results.notes: All five elements are supported. Nuances for narration: (1) 'Windows' in NLS meant split-screen/multiple windows with flexible view control, not the overlapping, draggable windows of later Xerox PARC/Apple GUIs; avoid implying a modern desktop window system. (2) The remote collaboration was with colleagues ~30 miles away at SRI in Menlo Park (Bill Paxton, Don Andrews and Jeff Rulifson appear via the live link, per the Brown CS telecollaboration page https://cs.brown.edu/stc/resea/telecollaboration/engelbart.html and others), carried over two microwave video links, with the mouse/keyboard data sent to the SDS 940 over homemade modems (sources disagree on 1200 vs 2400 baud; avoid citing a figure). (3) CHM's careful wording 'actual instances of, or precursors to' is a good model: the demo showed working versions or precursors of these ideas rather than 'inventing' them all on stage. (4) The demo also introduced the five-key chord keyset alongside the mouse, which the narration may want to mention. (5) Stewart Brand assisted with cameras/production (Wikipedia).

results.claim: The first mouse prototype was a wooden-shelled device built by Bill English in 1964 at SRI based on Engelbart's concept.

sources.title: The computer mouse and interactive computing
sources.supports: Bill English, then chief engineer at SRI, built the first computer mouse prototype in 1964 from Engelbart's design; SRI later patented it as an 'X-Y position indicator for a display system' (patent awarded 1970).

sources.title: Prototype Engelbart mouse (replica) - CHM Revolution
sources.supports: SRI engineer Bill English built the first Engelbart mouse prototype (circa 1964), which used knife-edge wheels and had space for only one button.

sources.title: The Mouse - Doug Engelbart Institute
sources.supports: The first prototype, a one-button mouse in a wooden shell on wheels, was built in the fall of 1964 to test the concept; Engelbart's idea was sketched in his notebook and English built it.

results.notes: Confirmed with precise framing: Engelbart conceived it (notes from 1961, sketch in his pocket notebook) and Bill English built it in fall 1964. Narration should credit Engelbart as inventor and English as builder/engineer, not say English 'invented' it. Material: CHM's acquisition note (https://computerhistory.org/sri-mouse-mn052024/) says the original was crafted from redwood by the SRI machine shop; some secondary sources say pine, so say 'wooden' or 'redwood' (CHM), not pine. Mechanism: two perpendicular knife-edge/sharp wheels, one button. Date discrepancy: Wikipedia's Bill English article says 1963; the Engelbart Institute, SRI and CHM all say 1964; use 1964. Also note the mouse on display in CHM's Revolution exhibit was for years a faithful replica made by English himself; CHM acquired the original in 2024, so archival photos may show the replica.

results.claim: The mouse used in the 1968 demo was a later three-button model, not the original 1964 wooden prototype.

sources.title: The Mouse - Doug Engelbart Institute
sources.supports: States the 1968 version included a three-button mouse and five-key keyset, distinct from the one-button wooden first prototype of 1964.

sources.title: The Mouse (Engelbart's account) - Doug Engelbart Institute
sources.supports: Engelbart in his own words: 'The mouse we built for the [1968] show was an early prototype that had three buttons'; the team experimented with up to five buttons and settled on three; the cord was turned to exit the top ('tail') to avoid tangling.

sources.title: Production-run three-button mouse, serial number 001 - CHM Revolution
sources.supports: By 1968 SRI had provided Engelbart with commercially produced three-button mice (production run, ca. 1968, made by Computer Displays, Inc.) to use in the 'Mother of All Demos'.

results.notes: Confirmed: the demo mouse had three buttons and was not the 1964 one-button wooden shell. Nuances: (1) Sources differ slightly on how to characterize the demo unit: Engelbart called it 'an early prototype' with three buttons, while CHM describes commercially produced/production-run three-button mice supplied for the demo. Narration should say 'a later three-button model' or 'a refined three-button mouse' and avoid both 'the original wooden mouse' and strong claims of a mass-produced commercial product. (2) The exact physical unit shown on stage is not firmly established; a Gizmodo piece on an auctioned three-button SRI mouse notes the demo footage shows a darker housing and provenance cannot be confirmed, so do not identify a specific surviving artifact as 'the demo mouse'. (3) A Logitech blog post claims the demo mouse was wooden and one-button; this contradicts Engelbart's own account and CHM and should be treated as a common error the narration must avoid. (4) The three-button design became standard except on the Mac (Engelbart's account).

challenges.claim: Douglas Engelbart and his SRI team gave the demonstration later called "The Mother of All Demos" on December 9, 1968, in San Francisco (Fall Joint Computer Conference).
challenges.reason: Could not refute. Every source checked (Doug Engelbart Institute, IEEE/ETHW milestone, Computer History Museum, SRI, Wikipedia) agrees on December 9, 1968, at the ACM/IEEE Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco, session title 'A Research Center for Augmenting Human Intellect', ~1,000 attendees. The name was applied retroactively (the claim already says 'later called'), which is accurate. Only nuance found: the venue was the San Francisco Civic Auditorium (now Bill Graham Civic Auditorium); some accounts say 'Brooks Hall', which ETHW flags as an error. The claim does not name the hall, so no correction is needed.
challenges.better_wording: On December 9, 1968, at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco's Civic Auditorium, Douglas Engelbart and his SRI Augmentation Research Center team gave the 90-minute demonstration later nicknamed 'The Mother of All Demos'.

challenges.claim: The 1968 demo showed a mouse, hypertext links, on-screen text editing, windows, and real-time collaboration/video conferencing with remote colleagues.
challenges.reason: Could not refute. SRI's own history lists hypertext linking, real-time text editing, multiple windows with flexible view control, and shared-screen teleconferencing; the ETHW milestone and DEI confirm the mouse's first public showing and the audio/video link to colleagues about 30 miles away at SRI in Menlo Park, whose faces appeared on screen while they jointly worked on the shared display. Two nuances worth noting but not errors: (1) 'windows' here means NLS's split-screen multiple views, not overlapping GUI windows of the later Xerox PARC/Mac style; (2) the 'video conferencing' was a shared-screen session with a live video/audio link (the remote colleague's face superimposed on the display), carried over leased video links and homemade 1200-baud modems, rather than a standalone videoconferencing product.
challenges.better_wording: The 1968 demo showed the mouse in public for the first time, along with hypertext linking, real-time on-screen text editing, multiple on-screen windows (split-screen views), and shared-screen collaboration with a live audio/video link to colleagues 30 miles away at SRI in Menlo Park.

challenges.claim: The first mouse prototype was a wooden-shelled device built by Bill English in 1964 at SRI based on Engelbart's concept.
challenges.reason: Could not refute, but there is a real dating disagreement to be aware of. The Doug Engelbart Institute, SRI, and the Computer History Museum catalog (object 102803057) all say Bill English built the first prototype in 1964, in a wooden (CHM says redwood) shell with two perpendicular wheels and one button, from Engelbart's sketch. However, Wikipedia's Bill English article, the Science Museum (London) replica record ('Computer mouse prototype, 1963'), and a 2020 Vancouver Sun obituary give 1963; Engelbart's own notes mention a 'bug' device in November 1963, and Engelbart dated the original idea to 1961. The claim's 1964 matches the primary institutions (DEI, SRI, CHM), so it stands, but a hedge is advisable. The wood species is also disputed (redwood vs pine); 'wooden-shelled' sidesteps that correctly.
challenges.better_wording: The first mouse prototype, a one-button device in a carved wooden shell riding on two perpendicular wheels, was built by SRI engineer Bill English in 1964 (some accounts say late 1963) from a concept Engelbart had sketched in his notebook.

challenges.claim: The mouse used in the 1968 demo was a later three-button model, not the original 1964 wooden prototype.
challenges.reason: Could not refute. Engelbart himself said 'The mouse we built for the [1968] show was an early prototype that had three buttons. We turned it around so the tail came out the top,' and that the team tried up to five buttons before settling on three. The Computer History Museum's record for the Computer Displays Inc. production-run three-button mouse (serial 001, ca. 1968) states SRI had provided commercially produced three-button mice for the demo, and a DEI page identifies that production model as the one used at the FJCC. The sources disagree on whether the exact unit on stage was a hand-built prototype or a CDI production unit, but all agree it was a three-button device and not the 1964 one-button wooden prototype, so the claim holds. The word 'model' is appropriately neutral on the prototype-vs-production question.
challenges.better_wording: The mouse used in the 1968 demo was a later three-button design (with its cord exiting from the top), not the one-button wooden prototype of 1964; sources differ on whether it was a hand-built prototype or one of the commercially produced three-button units SRI had by then.

results.claim: The Xerox Alto was developed at Xerox PARC with the first units operating in 1973; it was an experimental/research machine, not a mass-market product.

sources.title: Alto: A Personal Computer (Xerox PARC report CSL-79-11, Thacker, McCreight, Lampson, Sproull, Boggs)
sources.publisher: Xerox PARC, hosted by Computer History Museum (bitsavers)
sources.supports: Primary source: the Alto was 'designed in early 1973 as an experiment in personal computing'; the first prototype ran in April 1973 and Smalltalk was running on it by June 1973; by summer 1979 nearly a thousand Altos were in regular use by researchers, engineers and secretaries.

sources.title: Xerox Alto - CHM Revolution
sources.supports: Alto developed at Xerox PARC; lead engineer Charles Thacker noted the first unit cost Xerox $12,000; presented as a research machine, not a product.

sources.title: Alto (computer)
sources.supports: Alto developed at PARC with a GUI using a mouse and windows; Xerox only later introduced a commercial version, the Xerox Star, in 1981 (the Alto itself was never sold as a product).

results.notes: Date nuance: the PARC team's own 1979 report says the first prototype ran in April 1973; several secondary timelines (computinghistory.org.uk, historyofinformation.com) give 1 March 1973 as the 'introduction' at PARC. 'First units operating in 1973' is safe; avoid naming a specific day. Scale nuance: roughly 1,500-2,000 Altos were built over the following decade for Xerox labs and for universities (Wikipedia; IEEE Spectrum 'Still Living in the Xerox Alto's World'); it was never offered as a commercial product. Interface nuance: the Alto had a bitmapped display, three-button mouse, and (in Smalltalk) overlapping windows and pop-up menus, but the office 'desktop' of document/folder icons was developed for the Star; the icon concept itself grew out of Alto-era research (David Canfield Smith's 1975 Pygmalion thesis). Do not describe the Alto as having a Star/Mac-style icon desktop.

results.claim: The Xerox Star (8010 Information System) was released commercially in 1981 and had a desktop metaphor with icons, windows, and a mouse.

sources.title: Xerox Unveils Multipurpose Personal Information System (PR Newswire, New York, April 27, 1981)
sources.publisher: Xerox press release via PR Newswire, archived at tech-insider.org
sources.supports: Primary source: Xerox announced and demonstrated the 8010 Star information system on April 27, 1981 in New York; described a two-page desktop display, keyboard, processor and 'an unusual control device' (the mouse); U.S. price $16,595 with basic software.

sources.title: Xerox 8010 Star Information System
sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.supports: Development began in 1977 using Alto concepts; bit-mapped WYSIWYG GUI, two-button mouse, built-in Ethernet; the interface represented office objects (documents, folders, file drawers, in/out baskets) as icons; introductory price $16,595 per workstation.

sources.title: Xerox Star
sources.supports: Star introduced in 1981 as the commercial successor to the Alto with an icon-based graphical interface and mouse.

results.notes: Announced/released nuance: the firm date is the announcement, April 27, 1981 (press release); public showing followed at the National Computer Conference in Chicago in May 1981; first customer shipments came later in 1981 and no authoritative ship date surfaced, so narration should say 'announced/introduced in April 1981' rather than cite a ship date. Price nuance: $16,595 was for a single workstation; a working networked office system with file/print servers cost far more (often quoted around $75,000). Windows nuance: the original Star tiled its document windows rather than letting them overlap (the designers removed overlapping as confusing; see Smith et al. 1982 and mprove.de/visionreality/text/3.1.6_xeroxstar.html); overlapping windows came back in the later ViewPoint release. Name nuance: 'Star' was the software/system name, the 8010 workstation hardware was code-named Dandelion. Sales figures vary widely in sources (from under 2,000 to about 25,000 systems); avoid quoting a number. Also see CHM's 1981 'Final Demonstration of the Xerox Star' transcript: https://archive.computerhistory.org/resources/access/text/2015/09/102737965-05-01-acc.pdf

results.claim: The Apple Lisa was released in January 1983 with a graphical user interface.

sources.title: January 19: Apple Computer Introduces the Lisa (This Day in History)
sources.supports: Apple introduced the Lisa on January 19, 1983.

sources.title: The Lisa: Apple's Most Influential Failure
sources.supports: Lisa announced January 19, 1983 at $9,995 with a graphical user interface; a key stepping stone to the Macintosh; Apple engineers developed its GUI from scratch though influenced by Xerox PARC; discontinued April 1985.

sources.title: GUIdebook: Apple Lisa spotlight - Introduction (timeline)
sources.supports: Timeline entry: June 1983, Lisa begins shipping; September 1983 price cut to $6,995 without bundled software.

results.notes: Announced vs shipped: January 19, 1983 is the announcement/introduction date; at launch Apple promised delivery in May 1983 (Craig 1993 article hosted at bitsavers.computerhistory.org) and units actually began shipping in June 1983 (GUIdebook timeline and other secondary sources). Narration should say 'announced/introduced in January 1983' (or 'unveiled'), not 'shipped in January'. The Lisa was the first personal computer sold with a GUI by Apple, but not the first commercial GUI machine (the Xerox Star beat it to market in 1981, per CHM). The CHM catalog entry https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/102805342 also gives Jan 19, 1983 and $9,995. Lisa sold poorly (roughly 10,000 units by most accounts); CHM calls it 'Apple's most influential failure'.

results.claim: The Apple Macintosh was released in January 1984 and helped bring the GUI to a wider audience.

sources.title: A Computer for the Rest of Us
sources.supports: Macintosh introduced January 24, 1984; its graphical interface and mouse were new on mass-market computers.

sources.title: 1984 - Timeline of Computer History
sources.supports: Apple introduced the Macintosh in 1984 (heralded by the Super Bowl commercial) at about $2,500; described as the first successful mouse-driven computer with a graphical user interface.

sources.title: Graphical user interface (GUI)
sources.supports: After the expensive Lisa, the lower-cost Macintosh shipped in 1984 'won millions of converts' to the graphical interface.

results.notes: Date nuance: the Macintosh was unveiled by Steve Jobs on January 24, 1984 at Apple's annual shareholders meeting at the Flint Center, De Anza College, Cupertino, and went on sale at $2,495; the '1984' Super Bowl commercial aired two days earlier, January 22, 1984 (Smithsonian Lemelson Center: https://invention.si.edu/invention-stories/remembering-apples-1984-super-bowl-ad). 'Released in January 1984' is accurate. Framing nuance: it was not the first GUI computer (Alto 1973, Star 1981, Lisa 1983 preceded it); it is best described as the first commercially successful, affordable mass-market GUI/mouse computer. First-year sales were modest after a strong start (about 70,000 units by May 1984), so 'helped bring the GUI to a wider audience' is well supported; avoid 'instant success'.

results.claim: Apple did not invent the graphical user interface or the mouse; both predate Apple's products (SRI, Xerox PARC).

sources.title: The computer mouse and interactive computing
sources.supports: The mouse was developed at SRI by Douglas Engelbart's group in the early 1960s; Bill English built the first prototype in 1964; the basic patent (Engelbart named inventor) was filed in 1967 and issued in 1970; publicly demonstrated at the December 9, 1968 'Mother of All Demos'.

sources.title: Firsts: The Mouse
sources.supports: First mouse prototype (one-button, wooden shell on wheels) built in fall 1964 to test Engelbart's concept; patented 1970 as an 'X-Y Position Indicator'; first public demo December 1968.

sources.title: Xerox PARC - CHM Revolution
sources.supports: The Alto GUI (icons, mouse, windows) was developed at Xerox PARC in the 1970s; Apple engineers and Steve Jobs visited PARC in December 1979, which reinforced similar work already underway at Apple for the Lisa and Macintosh.

results.notes: Lineage: Engelbart's SRI lab (mouse, windows, hypertext, 1960s) -> several of his team moved to Xerox PARC in the 1970s (Alto, Smalltalk, Star) -> Apple (Lisa 1983, Macintosh 1984); Britannica's GUI entry states this chain explicitly. Mouse-date nuance: Engelbart's notes date to 1961, the concept is often dated 1963, the first prototype was built in 1964 (the Engelbart Institute now says attributing the build solely to Bill English was an oversimplification); say 'conceived by Engelbart in the early 1960s, prototyped 1964'. Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (1963) is another pre-Apple GUI precursor if the script wants one. Fairness nuance: Apple did not simply copy PARC. Xerox received Apple pre-IPO stock in exchange for the 1979 PARC demonstrations; Apple's Lisa and Macintosh projects were already underway; CHM notes Apple engineers built the Lisa GUI from scratch; and Apple contributed genuine innovations (menu bar with pull-down menus, drag-and-drop file manipulation, double-click, the desktop Trash). Lisa designers told Byte that 'the only thing we probably took from Star was icons' and that most of their Xerox inspiration was Smalltalk (quoted in Johnson et al. 1989: https://worrydream.com/refs/Johnson_1989_-_The_Xerox_Star,_a_Retrospective.pdf). Avoid the word 'stole'.

results.claim: The desktop metaphor with folder and trash/wastebasket icons was present on the Xerox Star (1981) and later Apple Lisa/Macintosh.
results.correction: The desktop metaphor with document and folder icons (plus file drawers, in/out baskets and printers) debuted commercially on the Xerox Star in 1981, but the original Star desktop had no trash/wastebasket icon; files were deleted with a keyboard Delete key. The on-screen trash can first appeared commercially on the Apple Lisa in 1983 (named 'Wastebasket', later renamed 'Trash') and then on the Macintosh in 1984 ('Trash'). Xerox added a Wastebasket to its own Star/ViewPoint desktop around 1985.

sources.title: Icon for wastebasket or the like (U.S. Design Patent D295632)
sources.supports: Xerox Corporation's design patent for a wastebasket icon was filed October 28, 1985 (inventors Doris Wells-Papanek, William Verplank, Norman Cox) and granted May 10, 1988, i.e., more than four years after the 1981 Star launch.

sources.title: Xerox Star (GUI Gallery)
sources.supports: States that the original 1981 Xerox 8010 Star desktop does not have the 'Waste Basket'; deletion was performed with the keyboard Delete key.

sources.title: Trash (computing)
sources.supports: The Apple Lisa shipped in 1983 with a 'Wastebasket' icon (later renamed 'Trash'); the Macintosh (1984) refined it as 'Trash'; in Apple v. Microsoft the court held Apple's trash icon to be original, protectable expression.

results.notes: The folder part of the claim is solid: the Smithsonian's 8010 Star entry (https://americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object/nmah_1064205) and Smith et al.'s 1982 Byte article 'Designing the Star User Interface' (https://guidebookgallery.org/articles/designingthestaruserinterface) document document, folder, file-drawer, in/out-basket and printer icons; Norm Cox drew the final icons and David Canfield Smith originated the office/desktop metaphor. The trash part is not: Xerox's own documentation first shows a Wastebasket in the September 1985 ViewPoint Application Developer's Guide (section 2.6, https://kuiper.mirrorservice.org/sites/www.bitsavers.org/pdf/xerox/viewpoint/programming/610E00200_Viewpoint_Application_Developers_Guide_Sep1985.pdf), consistent with the October 1985 design-patent filing. Some popular articles (e.g., AV Club) date the trash icon to the 1981 Star, but no primary Star 1.0 documentation or screenshot supports that, and the Apple v. Microsoft ruling treating Apple's trash can as original points the same way. Apple naming nuance: Lisa called it 'Wastebasket' (an alley-style can with tipped lid), a later Lisa update and the Macintosh called it 'Trash' (Susan Kare's closed-lid can). Suggested narration: credit the Star with the icon desktop (documents, folders, in-baskets, printers) and credit the Lisa/Macintosh with the trash can.

challenges.claim: The Xerox Alto was developed at Xerox PARC with the first units operating in 1973; it was an experimental/research machine, not a mass-market product.
challenges.reason: Holds. Sources consistently date the first Alto to spring 1973 (Wikipedia/DigiBarn give March 1, 1973; IEEE Spectrum says early spring 1973; the design memo is dated December 19, 1972). Roughly 2,000 units (120 Alto I, ~2,000 Alto II) were built over about a decade, used inside Xerox and donated to universities (MIT, Stanford, CMU, Rochester, c. 1978-79); Xerox rejected proposals to market it and it was never sold as a product. Only one outlier (mprove.de) says Altos became operational in 1974, which is contradicted by the project's own chronology. Minor nuance: it was not a one-off prototype but a production run of ~2,000 research machines, so 'experimental/research machine' is accurate as long as it is not read as 'a single prototype'.
challenges.better_wording: The Xerox Alto was developed at Xerox PARC, with the first machines running in spring 1973; roughly 2,000 were built for use inside Xerox and at a handful of universities, but it was never sold commercially.

Apple announced/unveiled the Lisa on January 19, 1983 (base price $9,995), but it did not ship to customers until June 1983; Apple had originally promised May delivery. Multiple sources (Wikipedia, Low End Mac, GUIdebook timeline, AppleMatters) agree on the June 1983 shipping date. Saying it was 'released' in January is therefore imprecise: the product was introduced in January and released (shipped) in June. The GUI part of the claim is correct.

challenges.claim: The Apple Macintosh was released in January 1984 and helped bring the GUI to a wider audience.
challenges.reason: Holds. Steve Jobs unveiled the Macintosh at Apple's annual shareholders meeting at the Flint Center, Cupertino, on January 24, 1984, two days after the '1984' Super Bowl ad, and unlike the Lisa it went on sale that same day at $2,495 (about 70,000 sold by May 3, 1984). At $2,495 versus the Lisa's $9,995 and the Star's ~$16,595 per workstation, it did bring the GUI to a far larger audience, so the second part is a fair characterization. Nuance only: initial sales slowed later in 1984, so 'helped bring to a wider audience' is appropriately hedged; it did not make the GUI dominant overnight.

challenges.claim: Apple did not invent the graphical user interface or the mouse; both predate Apple's products (SRI, Xerox PARC).
challenges.reason: Holds. The mouse was conceived by Douglas Engelbart and built by Bill English at SRI in 1963-64 (patent granted 1970) and demonstrated publicly in the 1968 NLS demo; GUI antecedents include Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (MIT, 1963), Engelbart's NLS (tiled windows, 1968), and the Xerox PARC Alto (1973) and Star (1981), all before the Lisa (1983) and Macintosh (1984). Apple's team visited PARC in 1979 and Apple licensed SRI's mouse patent (Engelbart recalled roughly $40,000). Nuance, not a refutation: Apple did contribute genuine GUI innovations of its own (e.g., the menu bar with pull-down menus, drag-and-drop, the one-button mouse made cheap), so the claim should not be read as 'Apple merely copied'. Also the lineage is broader than SRI and PARC alone (MIT's Sketchpad).
challenges.better_wording: Apple did not invent the mouse (Engelbart and English at SRI, 1963-64) or the graphical user interface (Sketchpad at MIT 1963, Engelbart's NLS 1968, Xerox PARC's Alto 1973 and Star 1981); Apple licensed the SRI mouse patent and refined and popularized these ideas in the Lisa and Macintosh.

results.claim: Tim Berners-Lee wrote the proposal for what became the World Wide Web at CERN in March 1989.

sources.title: Information Management: A Proposal (Tim Berners-Lee, CERN, March 1989, May 1990)
sources.supports: The original document itself, written at CERN and dated March 1989 (the W3C copy notes it was redistributed unchanged apart from a May 1990 date); proposes a distributed hypertext system; Berners-Lee notes the only name he had for it then was 'Mesh'.

sources.title: Web30: the 30-year anniversary of an invention that changed the world
sources.supports: CERN marks 12 March 1989 as the day Berners-Lee submitted 'Information Management: A Proposal' to his supervisors; CERN celebrated the 30th anniversary on 12 March 2019.

sources.title: First outline of the World Wide Web
sources.supports: CERN's own timeline entry for the March 1989 proposal, including Mike Sendall's 'Vague but exciting...' annotation and the fact that a revised version followed in 1990.

results.notes: Nuances for narration: (1) The 1989 document was titled 'Information Management: A Proposal' and did not use the name 'World Wide Web' — Berners-Lee's working name was 'Mesh'; the name 'WorldWideWeb' appears in the second, more concrete proposal he wrote with Robert Cailliau in November 1990. (2) The proposal was not approved immediately; his boss Mike Sendall wrote 'Vague but exciting...' on the cover, and Berners-Lee recirculated it in May 1990 before getting the go-ahead (hence the 'March 1989, May 1990' dates on the W3C copy; CERN Archives https://archives.web.cern.ch/?p=609 also holds the annotated original). (3) CERN uses 12 March 1989 as the Web's 'birthday'; it is the date of the proposal, not of any working software or site. Proposal (1989) is distinct from first server/site (Dec 1990) and public announcement (Aug 1991).

results.claim: The first website (info.cern.ch) went live at CERN in 1991 and was served from a NeXT computer; the World Wide Web is distinct from the Internet, which predates it.
results.correction: The first website, info.cern.ch, was running on Tim Berners-Lee's NeXT computer at CERN by December 1990 — CERN dates the first browser/editor, server and website going live to December 1990, with the first full demonstration around Christmas 1990 — and the project was first announced to the wider Internet on 6 August 1991, when Berners-Lee posted it to the alt.hypertext newsgroup. The World Wide Web is distinct from the Internet, which predates it: the Internet (originating with ARPANET in 1969) had been in use for two decades when the Web was built on top of it.

sources.title: The world's first browser/editor, website and server go live at CERN
sources.supports: CERN's timeline places the first browser/editor, website and server going live at CERN in December 1990 (by Christmas 1990 HTML, HTTP and URL were defined and the first browser/editor and server software written), i.e., not 1991.

sources.title: A short history of the Web
sources.supports: States that info.cern.ch was the address of the world's first website and web server, running on a NeXT computer at CERN; the first server and browser were up and running at CERN by the end of 1990; CERN restored the first website at info.cern.ch in 2013.

sources.title: Sir Berners-Lee announces the WWW software on the Internet
sources.supports: The first public announcement was on 6 August 1991 to the alt.hypertext newsgroup, with instructions for obtaining the WWW software from CERN — the 1991 date is the public release/announcement, not the first site going live.

results.notes: The NeXT and info.cern.ch parts are confirmed (the NeXTcube, with its 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!' sticker, is held by CERN and was lent to London's Science Museum for the 25th anniversary: https://blog.sciencemuseum.org.uk/happy-25th-birthday-world-wide-web). The date needs care: CERN's timeline says only 'December 1990'; secondary sources commonly give 20 December 1990 (some say 24/25 December), and Berners-Lee's own account says the browser/editor was talking to the info.cern.ch server by Christmas Day 1990 (Scientific American, https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/facts-about-the-webs-creation). 6 August 1991 (alt.hypertext post) is often mis-stated as the day the first website went live; CERN frames 1991 as the year the Web 'spread beyond CERN' (https://home.cern/news/news/computing/month-1991-web-spreads-beyond-cern). The server's original hostname was nxoc01.cern.ch, with info.cern.ch as an alias. Web vs Internet: CERN's 'Where the web was born' page (https://drupal-home.web.cern.ch/science/computing/where-web-was-born) notes the Internet had existed since the 1970s when the Web was proposed, and Berners-Lee combined hypertext with the existing Internet; ARPANET went live in 1969 (https://www.livescience.com/20727-internet-history.html). Narration should say 'first website running at CERN by December 1990; announced publicly in August 1991' and not say Berners-Lee invented the Internet.

sources.supports: Quotes Norman's 1998 email: 'I invented the term because I thought Human Interface and usability were too narrow: I wanted to cover all aspects of the person's experience with a system, including industrial design, graphics, the interface, the physical interaction, and the manual,' and reproduces Tom Erickson's 1993 Apple meeting notes describing the 'Architect's office'.

(4) Do not say 'UX' was used at Apple then; Norman says it was not. (5) Norman later became VP of Apple's Advanced Technology Group (1995–1997) and has since lamented that 'user experience' has become a misused buzzword.

results.claim: Multi-touch technology predates the iPhone (e.g. Bill Buxton's 1980s research at University of Toronto, FingerWorks, Jeff Han's 2006 demonstrations).

sources.title: Multi-Touch Systems that I Have Known and Loved
sources.supports: Buxton's first-hand history: his Toronto group was working on multi-touch in 1984 and publicly demonstrated a capacitive multi-touch tablet in 1985 (Lee, Buxton & Smith, CHI '85); notes Bob Boie's Bell Labs multi-touch display preceded it; records that FingerWorks (Wayne Westerman) was acquired by Apple in 2005, two years before the iPhone.

sources.title: Jeff Han: The radical promise of the multi-touch interface (TED2006)
sources.supports: Han's multi-touch demo was given at TED2006 in February 2006, roughly a year before the iPhone announcement.

sources.title: FingerWorks
sources.supports: FingerWorks was founded in 1998 by John Elias and Wayne Westerman at the University of Delaware, sold multi-touch products (iGesture Pad, TouchStream keyboard), and was acquired by Apple in 2005; Westerman and Elias joined Apple.

results.notes: The claim is correct and the three examples are well chosen. Precision nuances: (1) Buxton's Toronto work: the multi-touch tablet was built in 1984 and publicly disclosed/demonstrated and published in April 1985 (Lee, Buxton & Smith, 'A Multi-Touch Three Dimensional Touch-Sensitive Tablet', CHI '85) — say 'mid-1980s' or '1984-85' rather than a single year. Buxton himself stresses the Toronto tablet was not the first: Nimish Mehta's camera-based 'Flexible Machine Interface' at Toronto (1982) and Bob Boie's capacitive multi-touch screen at Bell Labs (c. 1984) preceded or paralleled it; Buxton is better described as a pioneer and chronicler than 'the inventor'. (2) FingerWorks: founded 1998 (a Purdue alumni bio says 1999) by Wayne Westerman and John Elias, University of Delaware; shipped the iGesture Pad and TouchStream keyboard; Apple acquired it in 2005 (announced it was out of business in June 2005) and Westerman became lead inventor on many Apple multi-touch patents — this is the direct lineage into the iPhone. (3) Jeff Han: the underlying FTIR technique was published at UIST in October 2005 ('Low-Cost Multi-Touch Sensing through Frustrated Total Internal Reflection'); the famous public demo was TED2006 in February 2006 (Monterey), followed by a 16-foot multi-touch wall at SIGGRAPH 2006 Emerging Technologies. So '2006 demonstrations' is accurate if referring to the demos; the research paper is 2005. Han went on to found Perceptive Pixel.
